title: Five Spooky Sky Targets to Spot This Halloween
summary: Halloween is a great time to look up at the night sky. You need no telescope for these targets, just a dark sky and patience. First, find the Pleiades, a group that looks like six or seven bright stars. With binoculars you can see dozens more from a cluster of about 1,000 stars. Celtic druids once marked Samhain, an early Halloween, by the Pleiades. From the United States, find Orion's Belt, follow a line up to orange Aldebaran, then look higher. Next is Algol, the Demon Star, in Perseus. It is really two stars orbiting each other; every 2.867 days one passes in front of the other, making Algol about 3.3 times dimmer for 10 hours. It will not be eclipsed on Halloween night in 2026, but dimming may show near October 29 and November 1. Then look southeast after sunset for Cetus, the sea monster near the Pleiades. Around the October 26 full moon, look for bright streaks around the Moon craters Tycho, Copernicus, and Kepler. Finally, watch for the bright, slow Taurid meteors streaking away near the Pleiades.
why_it_matters: Looking up at the stars is a free adventure you can start in your own backyard tonight.
